scenario: AITA for wanting to let my family know my daughter is getting married and post one or two pictures of the cake I'm baking on social media? | My daughter is getting married to her boyfriend of 2 years at the courthouse next week, while he's on leave from the army. This is not a shotgun wedding. They do not plan to have kids for the foreseeable future (if ever.) They intend to have a proper wedding in the future, when finances allow. However, in the meantime, she's forbidden me from mentioning it to anyone in our family or even friends of mine who know her, but do not know the family. These are kids who never had an apartment and want us (the parents) to give them what they need to get started. It's a financial imposition to ask us to furnish their house, and I know that both my family and the groom's family would be delighted to help if they could. In addition, the groom's family all knows this is going to happen and I feel our family will be terribly hurt if they are shut out completely. We're not inviting people to the courthouse, obviously, but they can call and offer their Congratulations anyway. I'm worried that, when they finally do have their wedding, nobody will want to come because they weren't even given the dignity of a notice. Further, I make lots of crafts and baked goods. I like to post the projects on social media for critiques and she's forbidden me from posting the wedding cake picture. Her real wedding will have a professional cake, but I wanted the practice, around just a few of us will be there. Frankly, my enthusiasm for helping her is dwindling and I am contemplating *not* baking the cake, as literally this exposure was all I wanted. I'm also thinking of offering her less for setting up house. My original thinking was, they could save up faster if they don't have to buy furniture and dishes. But she won't let us enlist the help of others. We have to replace what we give her and do without in the meantime, because we don't have money to buy these things right now. We're willing to do this for their comfort. It sure would be nice to see if anyone else is planning on getting rid of some old furniture or dishes so they can get started. Am I being an asshole?

Her real wedding will have a professional cake, but I wanted the practice, around just a few of us will be there. Frankly, my enthusiasm for helping her is dwindling and I am contemplating *not* baking the cake, as literally this exposure was all I wanted. But she won't let us enlist the help of others. We have to replace what we give her and do without in the meantime, because we don't have money to buy these things right now. Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (YTA - Yes, you're being an asshole)** **Here's why:** ### 1️️ **You're prioritizing your own need for validation over your daughter's boundaries** - Your daughter explicitly asked you **not** to announce the wedding or post about the cake. This is her decision as an adult. - **Why it's wrong:** - She’s likely trying to *protect* both families from financial pressure (e.g., "I don’t want relatives feeling obligated to gift furniture"). - Forcing her to "share" the news against her wishes is a violation of trust. It’s not about "dignity" — it’s about ** her autonomy** over her own life. - *Example:* If a friend asked you not to post about their divorce, would you post it anyway "because people deserve to know"? No. Boundaries exist for a reason. ### 2️️ **"Withholding help" as punishment is toxic** - You’re considering *not* baking the cake or reducing financial support **because she won’t let you post on social media**. - **Why it's wrong:** - This is **emotional manipulation**. Your love and support should be unconditional, not conditional on her compliance with *your* desires. - If you’re "dwindling enthusiasm" over a cake, ask yourself: *Is this about her, or about your need for social validation?* - *Real solution:* Bake the cake *for her* ( privately, no photos), and say: "I’m so happy for you. I’ll keep this between us, but I’m here for you however you need." ### 3️️ **"Dignity" is not a valid reason to bypass her wishes** - You worry: "If we don’t announce it, no one will come to the future wedding." - **Why it's wrong:** - **Her future wedding is her choice.** If she wants a small, intimate ceremony later, that’s her right. - *Reality check:* Most people understand " we’re eloping now, but will have a proper celebration later." *Not* announcing it now doesn’t mean " no one will come" — it means *she’s in control of the narrative*. - *Example:* If a couple elopes, family members don’t boycott their future wedding because " they didn’t tell us in time." They’re just happy for them. ### 4️️ **The " financial imposition" is your own assumption** - You assume family " would be delighted to help" — but ** she’s the one living this reality**. - *Her perspective:* - " I don’t want to burden my in-law family with furniture costs." - " I don’t want people feeling obligated to give gifts I didn’t ask for." - " I want to start my marriage without pressure or expectations." - **Your role as a parent:** Support * her* vision, not your own. If she doesn’t want help with furniture, *respect that*. If she *does* want help later, she’ll ask. ### ✨ **What you should do instead:** - **" I love you. I respect your wishes. I won’t post anything or tell anyone. I’m here for you, no strings attached."** - Bake the cake ** privately** ( no photos, no social media) as a gesture of love *for her*, not for external validation. - If you * want* to help with furniture, say: " We’d love to help you set up your home when you’re ready. No pressure — just let us know what you need." - **Remember:** A parent’s job is to *support* their child’s choices, not to *control* them. Your frustration is human, but acting on it by defying her boundaries is where you crossed the line. > **Final thought:** > * " I’m not an asshole for feeling hurt, but I *am* an asshole for trying to force my needs onto her. Her wedding is hers. My role is to love her, not to make it about me."* > **— YTA (Yes, you’re being an asshole for these specific actions)**. > *P.S. — This is fixable. Apologize, respect her boundaries, and focus on being her ally, not her audience.* 💛
